title: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez announces decision to freeze her eggs
summary: US congresswoman to share journey online as she criticizes Trump administration’s attacks on reproductive care
body: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has announced she is going to freeze her eggs and will be sharing the process online. The progressive New York congresswoman, 36, revealed her decision to undergo fertility treatment in a series of Instagram stories this weekend. “This is a choice that I am making to feel more in control of my life,” Ocasio-Cortez said. Ocasio-Cortez said she had been saving for the procedure for a very long time, and said there was not a lot of information for women interested in doing so. “As women in general, we are not taught about our bodies, we are not prepared for our own lives, whether that is in puberty, whether that is in pregnancy, whether that is in perimenopause, menopause, whether that is in so many different aspects of our lives,” she said in one of the stories. Ocasio-Cortez recognized the balancing act that comes with undergoing fertility treatment with her work as a congresswoman. Ocasio-Cortez told viewers that she would be taking her shots in the dressing room before a scheduled ABC interview on Sunday. “I want you all to see that,” Ocasio-Cortez said. “Because women can do anything. And I think it’s badass that I’m gonna be giving myself shots in the green room, get my glam on, roll out, talk international events, domestic policy, elections, pop out, live my life, do my thing.” Ocasio-Cortez also showed the medicines and tools, such as syringes and alcohol wipes, used in the process, which involves injecting multiple forms of medication over a period of time that typically lasts around 10 days or more. She joked she would not be injecting herself on a live feed, quipping: “Maybe I should start an ASMR egg-freezing channel.” “Don’t be weird about this, even I know though all of you will be,” she said with a slight smile moments before finding an injection site on her abdomen. She exhaled, injected the medication, and then remarked: “That wasn’t so bad!” During her Sunday interview on ABC, Ocasio-Cortez discussed her decision further. “In this political environment where this administration is denying reproductive care to women across the country, from abortion rights to the ability to carry out a healthy pregnancy, I think it’s important for us as leaders to have these conversations and share these processes, especially for working women across the country and normalize them,” she said. Ocasio-Cortez’s announcement drew praise. Amanda Litman, co-founder and president of Run for Something, a political action committee that supports young progressive candidates, said on X: “I’m just so grateful for her honesty & vulnerability.” Xochitl Hinojosa, a Democratic strategist, responded to Litman’s post by saying: “THIS. We don’t talk about women freezing their eggs or what women have to go through to start a family. Thank you @AOC for your bravery.”

title: Burnham vows crackdown on ‘rip-off’ business practices to ease cost of living
summary: First of PM’s ‘everyday fixes’ to be banning fake discounts and making it easier to cancel unwanted subscriptions
body: Andy Burnham has promised a series of measures to tackle the cost of living, including a ban on fake discounts and making it easier for people to escape unwanted subscriptions. The crackdown on “rip-off” business practices is expected to benefit consumers to the tune of £400m a year and will be the first in a range of “everyday fixes” to be implemented in the coming months. Writing for the Guardian, the prime minister said his government would step in wherever it could as he sought to put the cost of living at the heart of his premiership. “We won’t be able to solve every frustration overnight,” he wrote. “But where the government can save people money, remove an unnecessary obstacle or simply make something work better, we should and we will.” The government will ban misleading pricing practices that retailers use to make discounts appear better than they really are, including fake “was” prices, invented reductions and misleading recommended retail prices. Ministers will consult in the autumn on the precise practices covered and how the ban will work, before introducing the changes through secondary legislation. Downing Street hopes the measures can be implemented as soon as possible and does not expect a lengthy parliamentary process. The changes are intended to stop retailers inflating the price of an item before cutting it to give shoppers the false impression they are receiving a bigger discount. Burnham wrote: “If something is advertised as half price, it should actually be half price. We’ll make sure that when families snatch a deal, they can be confident they’re actually saving. That’s the least they deserve when budgets are so tight.” The government is also speeding up new protections against subscription traps, bringing forward their introduction from next spring to January. The rules will force businesses to provide clearer information when people sign up, regularly remind customers about their subscriptions and make it easier for them to cancel. Customers will also be given a 14-day cooling-off period after a trial ends or a long-term contract renews. The average person has about three subscriptions and spends about £500 a year on them, according to government figures. There are about 155m active subscriptions across the UK, and about £1.6bn a year is spent on unwanted ones. Ministers estimate consumers will save an average of £14 a month for each unwanted subscription they are able to leave early. “Too many companies want you to sign up in seconds but then make it feel impossible to leave. It’s exhausting,” Burnham wrote. The challenge for the prime minister will be whether smaller consumer-oriented interventions can provide savings households notice when many are still under pressure. The two measures will be followed by more over the coming months as he attempts to show voters his government can make a noticeable difference to household finances. Burnham also promised “bigger plans to make life easier and fairer for people over the longer term”, but Downing Street has yet to set out what those will include. Burnham wrote: “As far as I’m concerned, whatever the size, big or small, if it’s a problem for you, it’s a problem for us. That’s why I’ve made it clear from day one that creating room to breathe is my number one priority, and the whole of government is united on that. “Every single unexpected payment, rip-off or hidden catch chips away at hope. That might sound dramatic – but it’s true. Every single one is another message that thiscountry is built to catch people out rather than help them get on.” Citizens Advice welcomed the changes but said they “can’t be the end of the story”. The announcement comes as Burnham prepares to spend the rest of his summer travelling around Britain in an attempt to reconnect the government with voters, particularly in areas where Labour has lost support. “I’ll be asking people what action they want to see on the cost of living,” Burnham wrote. “Because if we want to find the problems that make everyday life harder, we need to listen to the people dealing with them.” Downing Street has not said whether what Burnham hears on the tour will shape the next round of “everyday fixes”.

title: Netanyahu rejects US-led 15-point Gaza peace plan in rare public break with Trump
summary: Israeli PM says IDF will not withdraw until Hamas is disarmed and rebukes US pressure to end wars without his country’s buy-in
body: Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has rejected a US-backed 15-point peace plan for Gaza in a rare public break with Donald Trump. In a statement on Sunday, Netanyahu said that he was confronting a “wave of rumours about Israeli weakness and Israeli withdrawals on all fronts” and rebuked US pressure to end wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran without Israel’s buy-in. On Gaza, he said: “Israel does not accept the 15-point document. The IDF will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is disarmed. And when I say the disarming of Hamas, it means heavy weaponry, lighter weaponry, all weaponry. And we are talking about genuine disarmament, not fictitious disarmament. Right now, we are talking with the Americans about this issue.” Trump’s Board of Peace in July proposed the 15-point plan, which mandated that Hamas disarm in exchange for providing a full Israeli military withdrawal from the Gaza Strip and an eventual transition of power to an independent Palestinian National Committee. Trump had said that the agreement would be implemented in stages, but Netanyahu on Sunday said that he wanted a full disarmament first in order to implement the deal. The Israeli leader’s main target in his remarks was the US. Israel has emerged as a key stumbling block in the Trump White House’s plans to broker peace in the region, in Israel’s conflicts in Gaza and Lebanon as well as in the war begun by joint US-Israeli strikes on Iran. And Netanyahu, who is facing tough elections in October and pressure from hardliners in his own government, appears ready to test his relationship with Trump in public in order to shore up his reputation as a defender of Israel at home. Israel had already signalled that it would reject the US-led plan. Soon after Trump announced it last month, Israel stepped up its bombing campaign in the Palestinian territory – strikes killed 18 people last Sunday. Netanyahu’s office had previously indicated it would not back the plan, saying: “The version that has been made public does not reflect Israel’s positions.” But Sunday’s rejection was far more forceful and direct, and appeared targeted at the Trump White House, as Trump and Netanyahu both face difficult elections. “Unlike all those who lecture us, we do what needs to be done for Israel’s security, and we can and know how to stand our ground, even against our best friends when necessary,” Netanyahu said. The head of Trump’s Board of Peace hit back on Sunday, saying the plan remained the “only way forward”. Nickolay Mladenov, the board’s high representative for Gaza, told Israeli television: “The option we are offering today is the only way forward that ensures this tragedy does not happen again.” Netanyahu’s rejection is a blow to Trump’s desire to be seen as a broker of peace in foreign conflicts. With midterm elections set for October, the White House is desperate to negotiate a peace in Iran in order to reopen the strait of Hormuz and help bring down oil and petrol prices. But the conflicts in the Middle East are interconnected and parallel US efforts have continued to bring peace to Lebanon, where Israel has occupied land in what it says is a buffer zone against Hezbollah, and Gaza, where Gulf allies of the US have decried what they say is an ethnic cleansing campaign being carried out by Israel. Like US presidents before him, Trump has found that Netanyahu can be a difficult ally. Bill Clinton, after meeting Netanyahu for the first time in 1996, is reported to have said: “Who’s the fucking superpower here?” More recently, the Biden administration found that its concerns about the human toll in Gaza were ignored, but continued to publicly back Netanyahu and did not significantly suspend military aid to the country for fear of the political blowback that Netanyahu and his allies in the US could cause. In Trump, however, Netanyahu has found a far more unorthodox and unpredictable counterpart in the White House. Netanyahu is a natural ally for Trump, and he has attacked Democrats before the midterm elections for being weak on supporting Israel. Yet more broadly, support for Israel and its war in Gaza is eroding in the Democratic party, and the Republicans have a presidential frontrunner for 2028 in the vice-president, JD Vance, who is publicly sceptical of Israel and the war in Gaza. Trump will have to decide whether to increase pressure on Netanyahu, potentially alienating some pro-Israel allies, or to allow his efforts for a Gaza peace plan to stall, perhaps indefinitely. The answer will depend heavily on the US president’s own political instincts – are US voters hoping to see Trump emerge as a statesman capable of ending one of the world’s bloodiest recent wars in Gaza, or would a public clash with Netanyahu provoke a revolt among his base? With both countries entering tumultuous election cycles and a generational shift in support for Israel among US voters, the result could redraw the alliance between Israel and the US.

title: Netanyahu rejects Trump’s Gaza plan and vows no withdrawal until Hamas disarms – as it happened
summary: This live blog is now closed.
body: We’re wrapping our live coverage of the Middle East crisis for today. Here are Sunday’s top developments: Israel has rebuffed Donald Trump’s Gaza plan. The country said it would not leave Gaza unless Hamas was “genuinely” disarmed. Israel Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said that they were discussing their concerns with the US. “They have ideas; some of them are acceptable to us and some are not, and we know how to stand our ground on these matters,” Netanyahu said. Donald Trump said he’s “low keying it” with Iran as the Strait of Hormuz remains closed. Trump’s comments to Axios came after Iran said it would not agree to a deal until the US met its demands, which included never speaking insulting the country. “We are only semi-negotiating with them,” Trump also told Axios. Although Donald Trump has rebuffed claims that the US is running low on weapons crucial to its war on Iran, a leaked memo indicates that his military leadership is concerned by falling stockpiles. Per the Washington Post, deputy US defense secretary Steve Feinberg on Wednesday told defense industry leaders that they must “drive significantly faster, more aggressive delivery schedules and/or increased production for critical capabilities.” Meanwhile, Trump’s war on Iran continues to draw prominent criticism in the US. New York’s Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said Trump’s complaints about rising costs clash with his policies that has made daily life more expensive. “Donald Trump may be saying that oil companies are making too much money, but what Donald Trump is doing is starting a reckless war in Iran, having closed door meetings with oil companies before his election, saying, you know, you give me money, you give me campaign contributions, and I will do whatever you want,” Ocasio-Cortez said on ABC. Iran’s supreme leader, Mojtaba Hosseini Khamenei, has selected a former commander of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps to represent him on the nation’s supreme security council, CNN reported. Mohsen Rezaei, whom CNN described as a “senior Iranian military adviser”, will replace Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr in this position, per CNN. Khamenei described Rezaei as a leader of the “Sacred Defense” which, CNN notes, is Iran’s way of referring to the 1988 Iran-Iraq war. In the official decree about Rezaei’s appointment, Khamenei expressed thanks to Zolghadr for his work. As CNN points out, it’s not known whether Rezaei’s appointment will affect Iran’s demands of the US to reopen the strait of Hormuz. An Israeli tank has invaded the town of Hadatha, southern Lebanon, with troops accused of setting buildings on fire, according to the Lebanese state-owned National News Agency. Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, recently met with supreme leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, who has not appeared in public since assuming the post early in the Middle East war, Khamenei’s office said on Sunday. “Dr Masoud Pezeshkian met Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei and spoke with him at the start of his third year in the presidency,” the supreme leader’s office said in a statement, without indicating the date of the meeting. Pezeshkian, who took office in July 2024, said in early May that he met with Khamenei, also without specifying the date, but the supreme leader’s office did not issue any statements at the time. The president had said on Wednesday that communication with Khamenei was “very difficult at the moment”, and speculation has swirled about the supreme leader’s health after he was reportedly wounded in strikes that killed his father. Khamenei’s office said the two “discussed in detail the country’s issues and problems”, including the “current military situation and future prospects”. Donald Trump on Sunday suggested that he’s going to let economic pressures prompt Iran to reopen the strait of Hormuz rather than launch another military action. “We are low keying it,” Trump told Axios. Trump’s comments came hours after Iran said that it wouldn’t reopen the crucial waterway unless the US met its demands – which included never insulting or threatening the country, per Axios. “We are only semi-negotiating with them,” Trump also told the news website. “We are just watching Iran with its huge inflation and the fact they have no money.” Trump, who said Iran “is in very bad shape”, claimed that Americans are feeling less financial pressures from the war because oil prices are down. “It will work out. It always works out. It’s like a chess game,” Trump also reportedly said. Donald Trump has rejected claims that the US is running low on munitions in its war with Iran – but a new report indicates that his military leadership is pushing defense companies to ramp up weapons production. According to the Washington Post, the deputy US defense secretary Steve Feinberg on Wednesday told defense industry heads that they must “drive significantly faster, more aggressive delivery schedules and/or increased production for critical capabilities.” Feinberg’s written directive to defense industry leaders said they had to present a plan within 21 days on how to increase production. Feinberg’s instruction was in a memo obtained by the Washington Post. “Years-long development cycles are not acceptable,” Feinberg reportedly wrote. “We must dramatically accelerate our program schedules and expand our production capacity now.” The Pentagon’s chief spokesperson, Sean Parnell, confirmed that this memo is “real” and “will inform the fiscal year 2028 budget submitted to Congress for funding, and it is entirely consistent with our ongoing push to rebuild the defense industrial base”, per the newspaper. Syria and Russia have made a deal about the Kremlin’s military presence in the Middle Eastern nation, according to reports. Russia has had a military presence in Syria since the Soviet era, but its standing there came into question after rebels ousted Bashar al-Assad some two years ago, according to the New York Times. Russia’s military presence featured two air bases as well as one naval port on the Mediterranean Sea. These bases and port were Russia’s “only supply and stopover hub in the eastern Mediterranean for planes and ships traveling to and from Africa,” the Times notes. Syria’s foreign ministry said Sunday they forged an agreement that “outlines a reorganized Russia’s presence on the Syrian coast, at the Hmeimim Air Base outside the city of Latakia and at the Tartus naval port”. The Syrian government has asked Russia to send back al-Assad. After al-Assad fled Syria, Russia gave him asylum. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, the New York progressive representative, discussed the Iran war’s impact on affordability during an interview airing Sunday, saying Trump’s complaints about rising costs don’t match his policies that make consumer goods more expensive. Ocasio-Cortez was asked on ABC’s This Week about her reaction to Trump’s comments that oil companies are “making too much money … based on a shortage” due to his war on Iran. “I think that every day people, every day Americans, we can see the very large gap between what Trump, Donald Trump says and what Donald Trump does,” Ocasio-Cortez said. “Donald Trump may be saying that oil companies are making too much money, but what Donald Trump is doing is starting a reckless war in Iran, having closed door meetings with oil companies before his election, saying, you know, you give me money, you give me campaign contributions, and I will do whatever you want.” “What he is doing is jacking up the price, not just at the pump, but at everything that you buy that requires the transportation of goods,” Ocasio-Cortez said. Donald Trump’s former defense secretary Mark Esper slammed Iran’s list of demands for reopening the strait of Hormuz, calling them “ridiculous” and saying they “should be rejected out of hand”. These include “demands such as the withdrawal of all US forces from the region, reimbursement for the costs of the war, the fact that we would end our blockade, we would end sanctions”, Espter said on ABC News’ This Week. “So it’s gone beyond the pale.” Esper’s comments on ABC come as Iran maintains a stranglehold on the important waterway. For Esper, Iran’s demands show “that they believe that they have the upper hand, they believe they are winning, and they are already. “That’s what we’re up against right now.” Iran has effectively instituted a blockage in the strait since the US-Israel war started in February and wants to charge tolls to ships that want to travel through. Iran has attacked vessels that it claims tried to get around this blockade. Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu rejected a Gaza plan hailed by US president Donald Trump, vowing no military pullout of Gaza until Hamas is “genuinely” disarmed. The Israeli military “will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed and will continue to thwart threats against our forces and our citizens,” Netanyahu said at a cabinet meeting. Here are the other key updates from today: The US must pressure Israel to accept the next phase of the Gaza plan, a Hamas official said, after Netanyahu rejected the US-backed agreement. “We expect the mediators and the American guarantor to pressure Netanyahu and his government to adhere to the roadmap and not obstruct the process for internal political and electoral reasons,” Hamas political bureau member Bassem Naim said. A Houthi drone salvo targeted a Saudi oil refinery on the Red Sea coast. The Iran-backed group’s military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the Houthis had “succeeded in targeting the Aramco refinery in Jazan on Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea coast with a drone”. Attacks by Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen killed at least four troops from the internationally-recognised government forces and injured 20 more personnel, two military sources said. The initial toll came from strikes on the Yemeni city of Mokha and surrounding areas, as well as Khokha, south of the port city of Hodeida, the sources said on condition of anonymity, after the H…

title: Zuckerberg faces questions over why superyacht reportedly declined to help stranded boat
summary: Small cruise ship rescued skiff in south-east Alaska even though Meta billionaire’s $300m megayacht was closer
body: Mark Zuckerberg has faced questions over why a small cruise ship in south-east Alaska rescued a stranded skiff and its crew when his 387ft superyacht had been closer. The Silicon Valley billionaire’s yacht, worth a reported $300m, is said to have “repeatedly” declined to assist when a nearby boat called for help last week. Zuckerberg, CEO of Facebook and Instagram owner Meta Platforms, was not on board at the time, a spokesperson told Forbes. When a nearby 21ft skiff ran out of fuel between Petersburg and Juneau, the Alaska Beacon reported operators of a cruise ship that was further away than Zuckerberg’s yacht came to the rescue. “I’m on a small-ship Alaska cruise with my son,” a passenger on the UnCruise Adventures ship Wilderness Legacy posted on Bluesky. “Our boat rescued a stranded vessel last night and apparently we did that after the Coast Guard radioed Mark Zuckerberg’s yacht – which was closer – and they repeatedly refused to respond. (There was near unanimous booing when the captain announced this).” But Brian Baker, a spokesperson for Zuckerberg and his wife, Priscilla Chan, told Forbes that the couple were not on board his yacht, named Launchpad. The yacht crew had been operating on a different radio channel, Baker told Forbes. “The assist was already under way” by the time they reviewed the broadcast, he said. Even if he was not on his ship, the report is unlikely to boost public opinion of Zuckerberg, who has faced criticism over the societal impact of his social media platforms; his new warm relationship with Donald Trump; and his lavish, insular lifestyle. “I live in Juneau and I’ve been having to look at that excessive eyesore parked up in [Auke Bay] for too long now,” a Reddit user wrote of the yacht in response to the rescue story. “Fuck Zuckerberg.”

title: Canadian government steps in as ‘out of control’ wildfires force thousands to flee
summary: British Columbia battling 102 fires day and night across province, as breakneck speed hampers firefighters’ efforts
body: Canada’s federal government has announced it will provide urgent assistance to British Columbia after an onslaught of unprecedented fast-moving wildfires forced about 22,000 people to flee their homes in frantic evacuations. A total of 102 wildfires were raging across the province on Sunday, of which nearly half were categorised as “out of control”, according to the BC Wildfire Service. Of those fires, 78 ignited during the past week. The entire community of Summerland, about 30 miles south-west of the city of Kelowna and home to about 12,000 people, was evacuated overnight on Saturday, along with a further 8,000 people around nearby Peachland. About 10,000 others have been told to prepare to evacuate at a moment’s notice. “I approved a request for federal assistance from British Columbia to provide shelter and accommodations for people who have been forced to leave their homes,” said Eleanor Olszewski, Canada’s minister of emergency management and community resilience in a social media post on Sunday. “I have tasked federal officials, led by the government operations centre at Public Safety ‌Canada, to work with the province to ensure support reaches those who need it most,” she said. Efforts to battle the Bald Range wildfire have been hampered by the breakneck speed of its spread. The blaze was first detected late on Friday evening, and grew within hours to more than 40 sq miles (100 sq km) – nearly twice the size of the island of Manhattan – as it raced nearly nine miles toward Okanagan Lake. The province’s premier, David Eby, declared a state of emergency late on Saturday, telling reporters that the blaze had been “like a bomb going off.” Cliff Chapman, BC Wildfire Service’s director of provincial operations, said the prolonged hot and dry weather the province has faced this summer had resulted in “explosive” fire conditions never seen before. Lightning caused by thunderstorms forecast this week could make the situation still worse, he said. Residents were shaken awake in the middle of the night to flee their homes. Jennifer Pascoa, who lives in Summerland, told the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation that she had begun to pack when she saw flames licking the nearby mountains. “It happened so quickly. We came home from the beach, we saw the plume of smoke, and then within an hour, the sky was covered in dark, black clouds,” she said. The British Columbia Wildfire Service said 10 standard helicopters and one night-vision helicopter were involved in the response, but had been hindered by thick smoke, turbulence and large fires. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police, the country’s federal police force, said they were investigating a possible fatality in the fire near Summerland. Mike Flannigan, a professor of wildland fire at Thompson Rivers University in Kamloops, BC, said the rapidity of the fires’ spread was indicative of increasingly extreme blazes springing up in Canada and the US. Southern BC and the pacific north-west in the US had had little to no rain in the past six weeks, leaving the regions “bone dry”, he said. “You walk through the forest, it crunches; if you look sideways, you start a fire.” These conditions were being driven by human-caused climate change, he said. “We’re seeing higher intensity fires today than the past … the shorter the timeframe, the more challenging it is.” Before this decade, fire agencies’ policy was that if a blaze was 20km (12 miles) away from a community, there was no cause for immediate concern. The ferocity and speed of these fires meant that such calculations no longer held, said Flannigan, warning that all homes in at-risk regions should have an emergency kit ready to go. “If a fire can run 60km in a day, you should be worried about it,” he said. The Bald Range fire was also an example of how fires could metastasise through the night, he said. Traditional firefighting practices would usually give firefighters a break during nightfall, as the cooler air would slow the burning. “That’s not the case any more. The fire roars through the evening, through the night, and we’re seeing this more and more,” he said. Drought and the sheer power and size of the fires during the day allow them to keep momentum even in the dark. Fire management agencies in BC and Alberta now fight fires after dark using night-vision helicopters. Current conditions indicated that the fire season in BC and the US states of Washington and Oregon could extend into the autumn, Flannigan said. “It looks grim … there’s no rain,” he said, adding that, like California, Canada may begin to have “fire years” instead of a summer fire season. “I’m scared for the coming weeks,” he said.

title: Alleged crime boss Daniel Kinahan’s return to Ireland ends global game of cat-and-mouse
summary: Kinahan built boxing empire while in exile in Dubai but now faces trial in Dublin charged with directing organised crime
body: A decade after escaping assassination and fleeing into exile, Daniel Kinahan is back in Ireland – but it is not the homecoming he wanted. The alleged leader of the Kinahan organised crime group was extradited from Dubai in an Irish government jet on Sunday and headed to a huge security operation in Dublin, marking the end of a global game of cat-and-mouse with European, US and Gulf authorities. The 49-year-old landed at Casement aerodrome in Dublin on Sunday evening and was taken to the criminal courts of justice in central Dublin to be charged with directing organised crime. A judge told Kinahan that, because of the charge, an application for bail would have to be made to the high court. Kinahan said: “I understand. I think we know I won’t be getting bail, but thank you.” He was then taken 50 miles outside the city to his new home in Portlaoise prison. Tabloid headlines anticipated his return with glee. “Du-Bye!” said one. “Dan and Dusted,” said another. “Kin Air: He’s Coming Home,” said another. It is a moment long sought by law enforcement agencies that named Kinahan as a leader of a cartel said to control about a third of Europe’s cocaine supply, along with running criminal sidelines in firearms and racketeering. As the founder of the boxing management company MTK Global the Dubliner was also an influential figure in sports and boasted of friendships with Tyson Fury and other champions. Kinahan has not been tried but is braced for conviction and a long sentence, according to clips of an interview that he gave by phone from Dubai to the podcaster James English. “I think I’ve already got life in prison. And we have to go through the dance now.” The married father of five said he had “not been an angel” but that accusations against him were overblown. “I believe in a way I’m a scapegoat.” He had not laundered money through boxing promotion, he said, rebutting one of the allegations against him. Kinahan said he looked forward to familiar Irish treats such as a crisp sandwich. “Get back home and have a little bit of batch bread and a packet of King crisps or Tayto.” The bravado, or fatalism, could not disguise a dramatic fall. From gilded opulence in the United Arab Emirates (UAE), allegedly at the helm of a criminal empire worth hundreds of millions of euros, Kinahan will reportedly become an inmate at the maximum-security A5 unit within A block at Portlaoise. His father, Christopher Kinahan, launched a family enterprise in the 1980s by importing heroin into Dublin. A polished figure with university degrees and a facility for languages, Kinahan senior, better known as Christy, was convicted of drug offences and money laundering while creating a network that spanned Latin America, north Africa, the UK and continental Europe. In 2009, a US diplomatic cable named his son Daniel as “an Irish businessman involved in narco-trafficking throughout Europe”. Soon after, Spanish authorities arrested Christy and Daniel and seized assets, but the Kinahans emerged largely unscathed. That changed when a murderous feud with the rival Hutch gang piled up corpses and led to an audacious but unsuccessful attempt on Daniel’s life at a boxing weigh-in at Dublin’s Regency hotel in February 2016. The death of one man, David Byrne, fuelled further killings. Kinahan was never again seen in public in Ireland and operated from southern Spain before settling in Dubai in the UAE, which had no extradition agreement with Ireland. With his father and brother Christopher junior, Daniel remained alert to surveillance attempts but lived openly and turned MTK Global into a boxing powerhouse. That apparent untouchability evaporated in 2022 when the US offered a reward of up to $15m for information that led to the arrest or conviction of the trio. Washington had been reluctant to get involved until lobbied by the then assistant garda commissioner John O’Driscoll, Greg Gatjanis, who ran the US national security council’s strategy for transnational organised crime, told the MacGill summer school last month. “To this day I hold Ireland, the gardaí, as the model [for international manhunts] of how they handled the Kinahan organisation,” said Gatjanis. “Their drug empire probably did not touch the US, but then he started talking about the effects of the Kinahan organisation and the terror they were inflicting. I went from telling him I couldn’t accommodate sanctions because I could not make a case for it to agreeing to starting up an investigation, and that began the entire sanction investigation.” In May 2025 Ireland agreed an extradition treaty with the UAE and the net began to close. Sean McGovern, a cartel lieutenant wanted for murder and directing organised crime, was extradited that month and jailed for 24 years. Daniel Kinahan was arrested in April this year. UAE authorities rejected his appeal last month, clearing the way for extradition. Irish military personnel are expected to reinforce police during Kinahan’s transfers to court and prison. Kinahan told the podcast he would be subject to a “circus” and “character assassination”. Gatjanis said no organised crime group lasted for ever. “It’s born, it crawls, walks, runs, starts to decline, ultimately dies.”

title: ‘I was on my honeymoon!’: Hamish Falconer’s surprise call-up to Burnham’s cabinet
summary: New EU negotiator, who previously helped free Taliban hostages, thought it was safe to book holiday during recess
body: When Hamish Falconer left his career as a Foreign Office diplomat for the hostile environment of a Labour party selection process, one of his last acts was a negotiation to free six hostages from the Taliban. When he won the key marginal seat of Lincoln in the 2024 general election, he did not expect to be back in those offices on King Charles Street quite so quickly – he was appointed Middle East minister just two weeks later. Two years on, he is one among the first three of his generation of MPs to reach the cabinet, and he is back around the negotiating table, this time with the EU. One of his oldest friends, Anneliese Midgley, is another of the three MPs from the 2024 intake to reach the cabinet, as Andy Burnham’s chief whip. Falconer had trusted Midgley – a close confidant of Burnham – to keep him in the loop about cabinet moves. But the tight secrecy of Burnham’s first appointment meant that he was caught off guard by his promotion, while on his honeymoon in Greece. “We got married in June but delayed the honeymoon until recess, and thought: what could possibly go wrong?” he said. “I thought it would be fine; Midge hasn’t told me not to go. Within 24 hours, I got a call saying: ‘Sorry, you have to look at flights.’ I was like: ‘I’m on my honeymoon!’ And the vibe was: you sort of have to be here for your first cabinet meeting. “So a combination of flights managed to get me back and forth, but on the 5am Jet2 flight, I might have been the only person wearing a suit.” He will attend cabinet as minister for European relations, taking the reins of negotiations with the EU for the next joint summit. While he is careful to praise his predecessor, Nick Thomas-Symonds, Falconer said he wanted to up the speed and ambition of deepening ties with the EU. “This is right at the centre of everything this government is trying to do: cost of living, energy,” he said. “Yes, there are some technical questions we need to get right. But the bigger picture is there is a massive wider European agenda. We want to be part of those discussions on security, defence, tech, about where Europe is going.” Falconer is the second generation of his family to attend cabinet – his father, Charlie Falconer, was Tony Blair’s justice secretary. He was long tipped as one of the most ambitious of the new intake of Labour MPs and has spent much of the past two years flying to summits and negotiations on Gaza and Iran. He has answered a record-breaking number of urgent questions in the House of Commons from MPs, on Israel and Gaza, Iran and Sudan and the Chagos Islands. “I found it so strange coming back into the Foreign Office, where apparently I still had stuff I had left there,” he said. “People I knew incredibly well, people I’d had dysentery with in South Sudan, they wouldn’t call me Hamish any more, they would only call me minister. So it was a real head-spin.” When Falconer took on the brief – nine months after the 7 October Hamas massacre and the subsequent Israeli onslaught on Gaza – there was deep suspicion of Labour because of Starmer’s early comments about the right of Israel to cut off energy and water to Gaza. Burnham has since apologised for how disillusioned many voters became with Labour over those comments. “I came in with this knowledge that there had been a lot of upset and concern about what Keir had said … the LBC interview, and so I was determined that we would make a real contribution,” Falconer said. “I feel so proud to be the first Middle East minister who recognised the Palestinian state. I will literally never forget the kids we helped rescue from Gaza, all the students who started their lives here.” But it never felt like enough, Falconer admits. Many in his party wished the government could have gone much further with evacuations, aid and sanctions. “It was a terribly difficult job to do for two years because I would feel that the country was desperate not to see the horrors of Gaza continue … they couldn’t bear – rightly – that there was malnutrition among children, that there was still terrible loss of life,” he said. “There are so many incidents that were burned into my mind. I think over the last two years we did really important and historic things. But nobody could look at the last two years in the Middle East and not feel just such a depth of sadness. And my God, I carried that with me, and will still carry that with me.” Falconer is speaking from his constituency office in Lincoln, yards from the cathedral in a city which is the sole patch of red in a county once solidly Conservative but where Reform have been growing dominant. It is home to the constituency of the Reform UK deputy leader Richard Tice, and the mayor is the former Conservative MP turned Reform UK defector Andrea Jenkyns. There is a palpable sense of relief from Falconer that Labour has some chance, under Burnham, to get another public hearing. “I can see what the alternative is. I see it every day. I work with a Reform mayor – actually that’s probably overstating how practical a conversation I can have,” he said. “I really know what is at stake because it is right outside my city, and this is such an important battle to get right. “The truth is, the right are not offering any answers for the country. I could have snorted with laughter at some of the proposals that were being made by Reform in recent weeks, which were so obviously unserious.” Burnham’s key weak spot has often been said to be foreign policy – and he has made it known he intends to spend far less time on the world stage than his predecessor, which has worried some officials and international leaders who admired Starmer’s commitment to Ukraine and to diplomacy in the Middle East. Falconer said it was “not fair” to describe the prime minister as uninterested. “I’ve known Andy a long time. He is incredibly engaged,” he said. “He’s someone who is good at forming relationships, and that’s so important in international relations.” But the “Makerfield test” should still be applied to foreign policy, how actions will affect the kinds of voters who delivered Burnham his landslide in his Wigan byelection. “It’s not a hard or complicated test,” Falconer said. “I am really focused on delivering something that my constituents will feel in their day-to-day lives. In my constituency office, I’m sat across from a small gas turbine producer. I want to make it easier for them to trade in Europe, to continue to grow. “I know through my job, I can make that better. That is true of businesses right across the city. That is what I think the Makerfield test, the Lincoln test, is all about.”

title: Labour seeking ‘deeper relationship’ with EU under Burnham, new minister says
summary: Exclusive: Hamish Falconer wants ‘sense of renewed pace’ in post-Brexit talks while staying within Labour’s red lines
body: The UK will move faster and be more ambitious on achieving closer ties with Europe under Andy Burnham’s government, his new chief post-Brexit negotiator has said. Hamish Falconer, the new cabinet minister in charge of the EU reset talks, said there was “room to be ambitious” within Labour’s red lines on Europe, which exclude reopening discussions on the single market and customs union, and he would look at the “art of the possible”. He said greater cooperation on services – which might include visa-free travel for British people working in the EU, or mutual recognition of qualifications – was the next big area where the UK hoped to make progress. “I would want a deeper relationship, a more ambitious relationship with the EU,” Falconer told the Guardian. “There’s also a whole range of areas in relation to services where I’d really like it to be progressed. Services is obviously an area where the EU itself is less closely integrated and there’s a lot of discussion within the EU about where to take the productivity challenge for them – that’s a challenge we can recognise here in the UK as well. So, particularly on services, I’m really interested in where we can go further.” Falconer, the son of the Labour grandee Charlie Falconer, is a former Middle East minister and diplomat who has experience as a Foreign Office negotiator. He said he wanted “a sense of renewed pace” in the talks – though there is still no new summit date in sight. The long-awaited reset summit, which had been proposed for July, was postponed after Keir Starmer resigned as prime minister in June. “We’re committed to our manifesto red lines, but all of my experiences as a negotiator and the art of the possible is in part shaped by the nature of the relationship between two people negotiating,” Falconer said. “I used to be a negotiator with the Taliban. With the EU, this is a negotiation with our friends, with whom we share our values and with whom we feel solidarity.” Earlier this summer, EU diplomats expressed concern that the talks under Starmer had lost momentum, with the second annual summit of EU and UK leaders repeatedly delayed as talks stalled over a youth mobility scheme. Falconer, who returned from his honeymoon when he was offered the post of Europe minister by Burnham, has spoken already to the EU trade commissioner, Maroš Šefčovič, and senior bloc figures hope he will bring a new energy to talks. One said of his predecessor Nick Thomas-Symonds: “I really liked him but the problem was the UK didn’t open up a window, create the political space for a deal.” They complained that instead of seizing opportunities to get a deal over the line and bank a political win to move on to the next phase, the UK negotiators “kept trying to add things” such as an agreement on services. A source close to Thomas-Symonds disputed this and said good progress had been made on all areas under discussion in advance of the planned July summit. It is believed that the next summit may not be held until October to give Falconer time to get across the detail, and for Burnham to flesh out his foreign policy. Resolving the terms of a youth mobility deal is a key priority, to allow tens of thousands of European and British young people to live and work in each other’s territories. Talks remained deadlocked due to the UK’s reluctance to allow EU students to pay the lower fees charged to UK students, something opposed by cash-strapped universities. Falconer said the deal should “work for both sides” and was mindful of financial pressures on the university sector. “In my constituency in Lincoln, there’s two universities. I’ve got those issues very much at the forefront of my mind,” he said. “It is vital that as we go through this, we have real respect on both sides for what some of the constraints are for each of us.” Falconer said he wanted to apply Burnham’s “Makerfield test” to the EU negotiations, ensuring they would deliver tangible change to ordinary people struggling with the cost of living, including in his own very heavily leave-voting constituency. But he said he would continuously emphasise principles of “European solidarity”, which he said went beyond trade and were backed by shared values, including on defence and security and on how countries could tackle growing dangers such as wildfires caused by the climate crisis. Starmer and Thomas-Symonds had been due to host the second UK-EU summit on 22 July, with progress already announced on a deal easing barriers for food and drink exports expected to come into force before summer 2027. Though there was a warm relationship between Starmer and the EU’s Ursula von der Leyen, the UK had also faced difficulty in fulfilling some of the promised changes agreed at the last UK-EU summit, including an inability to reach agreement on the UK’s entry into the €150bn Safe fund for defence investment. Talks over UK participation in Safe collapsed last November with France blamed for setting too high a price for British involvement. Seasoned observers in Brussels say it was also embarrassing for the EU and was “a failure of statecraft” on both sides. Falconer said: “I think that we have made some real initial progress on resetting but now we’ve got to deliver.” Having Downing Street support to give Falconer the political space that EU diplomats want created will be key. And he says he has the experience to deliver. “I used to be a negotiator in the Foreign Office, often doing really hard negotiations. Ultimately, the character of the wider relationship is really important,” he said. “Yes, there are some really important technical questions that we have got to get right.” “But we also need to put this in the big picture … there is also a massive wider European agenda, which is really important to us, and Britain is really important to that agenda too. Security, defence, tech. We are a big part of those discussions and those dilemmas.” Falconer said he would use his role – now at cabinet level – to boost the UK’s participation in solving Europe-wide challenges outside the EU. “We are part of Europe and we feel the threats to Europe, whether it’s in eastern Europe from Russia invading Ukraine, or even wildfires and that shared sense of challenge in dealing with that.”

title: Abdul El-Sayed embraces Trump claim he represents ‘very different’ America
summary: Michigan nominee, who spoke to Obama after primary win, vows to fight inequality as president ‘makes billions off you’
body: Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for US Senate in Michigan, embraced Donald Trump’s suggestion that the two represent “VERY DIFFERENT” versions of the US, pledging to fight inequality while the president is “making billions of dollars off of you”. In a Saturday night post on his Truth Social platform, Trump shared an image of himself and the first lady, Melania Trump, beside a photo of El-Sayed, who is Muslim, and his wife, Sarah Jukaku, wearing a hijab. “Two VERY DIFFERENT America’s [sic],” read the caption. “Yeah, he’s right,” El-Sayed told CNN, when asked about the post on Sunday. “One in which your overlords are two people who don’t like each other, but join in the interest of making billions of dollars off of you – or two people who genuinely love each other, enjoyed some pancakes together, want to come together to build the kind of America where they can raise a family and know that that family is going to have the good things.” “Yes, you’ve got two different visions of America,” said El-Sayed. “Donald Trump’s vision is the one you’re living in right now. Can you afford your gas? Can you afford your groceries?” El-Sayed, an epidemiologist, won the Democratic primary for US Senate in Michigan this week, setting up a bruising general election campaign against former US representative Mike Rogers, a Republican, in the swing state. His victory is widely seen as crucial to the Democrats’ hopes of retaking control of the Senate from Republicans. During a speech on Thursday, Trump called El-Sayed a communist and said he was “full of shit”, which was met with loud cheers. Asked about the president’s expletive remark, El-Sayed told Sky News: “At least I don’t let mine go in the middle of the Oval Office.” Unlike some other new Democratic candidates, El-Sayed, who ran to the left of his primary opponent, is not a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, and has said he is a capitalist who wants capitalism to work better. Former US president Barack Obama spoke with El-Sayed after his primary win, in what is deemed an early sign of support for his campaign. “It was a really good conversation about what we need to do to be able to win, and obviously this is somebody who knows a lot about winning Michigan,” El-Sayed told NBC News. Michigan backed both of Obama’s runs for the presidency, in 2008 and 2012, before voting for Trump in 2016, Joe Biden in 2020, and turning back to Trump in 2024. Obama also called Haley Stevens, the moderate Democrat whom El-Sayed defeated in the primary, Politico reported. Stevens urged the former president to “come to Michigan and campaign for the Democrats”, she told the outlet. Should he beat Rogers in November’s general election in Michigan, El-Sayed could become the first Muslim US senator. Republicans have described him as “the most radical Senate candidate in America”, and Trump has repeatedly used his full name, Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed. El-Sayed noted the party – and Trump – did the same to Obama, regularly including his middle name “Hussein” when referencing the former president. “At the end of the day it’s not radical to believe that people should be able to afford their groceries,” he told NBC’s Meet The Press. “It’s not radical to believe that you should have healthcare in this country. “It’s not radical … that you don’t think the president should be able to deny elections, or make $2.2bn out of his role in office. It’s not radical to believe all of us should be able to breathe clean air and drink clean water. Those are the things that I’ve been fighting for.” El-Sayed said: “They are going to try to paint me as a certain thing, given my name, but I also think it’s important to recognize that America has a long history of embracing, “America is a lot bigger than very small people like Donald Trump or [Vice President] JD Vance or Mike Rogers want to make it out to be. And so I’m grateful for all that America has given me.”

title: Pilot pulls off Count Binface stunt for Clacton byelection
summary: Plane spends 30 minutes off the Essex coast marking out shape of a bin in apparent tribute to Nigel Farage’s rival
body: A pilot has traced the shape of a bin with their flight path near Clacton before Count Binface challenges Nigel Farage in a byelection on Thursday. The light aircraft spent around half an hour between 2,100ft and 4,150ft above the sea near the Essex coastal town zigzagging to mark out the shape of a bin, according to data from Flightradar24. The plane took off from Earls Colne airfield near Colchester at 2.48pm on Saturday and landed at 4.13pm. The aircraft is in private ownership, according to Flightradar24, and the pilot’s identity is unknown. Voters will go to the polls in Clacton in a byelection triggered by the resignation of Farage, the Reform UK leader. Count Binface, a self-proclaimed space warrior who wears a bin-shaped helmet, is Farage’s main rival. There are also three candidates from the Official Monster Raving Loony party and numerous independents. All the main Westminster parties are boycotting the byelection, which they have dismissed as a stunt. A survey by Survation on behalf of Mandate Research suggests Farage will win 73% of the vote while Count Binface could get 20%. Farage resigned after it emerged that he was being investigated by the parliamentary standards commissioner over a £5m gift from the cryptocurrency tycoon Christopher Harborne, which he received before taking his seat in the Commons. The investigation, which is looking at whether he should have declared the money when he arrived in parliament, was suspended on his resignation but is expected to resume should he win the byelection. If he is found to have broken the rules, and a suspension of more than 10 days is imposed, it could trigger a recall petition and the prospect of the Reform UK leader losing his seat, forcing a further contest. Farage has repeatedly insisted the gift – revealed by the Guardian in April – was not linked to his political career. He has said he had no intention of returning to politics until June 2024, just before the election.

title: Let local communities be the stewards of their own wildlife
summary: Letter: Sjúrður Hammer responds to NatureScot’s decision to prohibit the annual Guga Hunt, where islanders collect gannet chicks on the Hebridean island of Sula Sgeir
body: What many celebrate as a win for nature conservation is, in my view, a significant step in the wrong direction for our relationship with the natural world (Scottish gannet chick hunt blocked for first time in 400 years, 3 August). The decision to prohibit the community on Lewis from collecting gannets runs counter to the spirit of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, which recognises that safeguarding biodiversity will not be achieved by scientists and city dwellers alone. Instead, it affirms that indigenous and local communities hold a legitimate and essential role as stewards and caretakers of their own environments. Too often, people in our part of the world assume that “indigenous and local communities” refers only to distant, exotic cultures or to the shameful legacies of colonialism. But the Kunming-Montreal accord makes clear that this category also includes small, place‑rooted communities in countries such as Scotland, the Faroe Islands and Iceland – communities with ancient traditions, distinct languages and ways of relating to nature that have endured for centuries. These cultures are not museum pieces; they are living, fragile social ecologies that are continuously pressured by the modern lifestyles and ethics of capitals and cities. As a seabird biologist who is also committed to the sustainable use of seabirds for food, I do not dispute the population modelling behind this decision, nor do I believe NatureScot has acted carelessly. But as a Faroe Islander, I have been on the receiving end of many conservation campaigns imposed from the outside, and I have seen how easily well‑intentioned policy can become a tyranny of the majority when local voices are sidelined. I would ask the Scottish government to ask themselves if they genuinely feel that the local community has been sufficiently and fairly heard in this matter, and if this decision has been taken in the spirit of the Kunming-Montreal accord. The guga hunt is a regulated, small‑scale practice embedded in local ecological knowledge. Ending it risks alienating the very communities that global biodiversity policy says must be empowered. Conservation that excludes local actors is not progress. Sjúrður Hammer Tórshavn, Faroe Islands • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

title: Why we should support welfare spending
summary: Letter: Labour peer Ruth Lister disagrees with the high number of party members looking to reduce spending on social security
body: The finding that 47% of Labour party members surveyed believe the government is spending too much on social security is depressing (Labour members ‘have tougher view on welfare than you might think’, poll suggests, 4 August). But perhaps it’s not surprising given the relentless false “out of control” political and media narrative, when in fact spending on non-pensioner social security has remained at about 5% of GDP for the past decade. Social security was one of the main victims of austerity, leaving benefits too low to meet basic needs – hence the increased reliance on food banks. If members had been presented with the evidence from academics, thinktanks and charities showing that improving social security represents the most effective way of tackling child poverty, I suspect they may have been more supportive of spending in this area. The Institute for Government has suggested that it should be seen as preventive spending, reducing the demand on acute services. I trust that the “senior strategists in Downing Street” with whom the survey findings were shared won’t take the wrong lessons from them. Ruth Lister Labour, House of Lords • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

title: How clean air clubs are protecting Americans from wildfire smoke
summary: Mutual aid groups that started giving out PPEs during COVID are now loaning air purifiers and distributing masks to fume-addled communities
body: Miquette Thompson’s home in rural Mendocino county has been covered in smoke all week. There are the nearby Feliz and Woodside fires in northern California, which have burned more than 1,000 acres, as well as the wildfires devastating Oregon and Washington that are sending smoke their way, too. “It’s become not unusual,” she said of walking outside and seeing a hazy sky. The wildfire smoke means dangerous air quality for her under-resourced, “wee rural little area”, Thompson said. Wildfire smoke is potentially unsafe for all populations, but particularly for elderly people and those with respiratory conditions. Hospitalizations for asthma go up 10% on smoke days, according to a recent University of California study. Having locally organized around safety amid airborne illness for years – distributing free personal protective equipment (PPE) to neighbors and Covid tests at farmers markets – Thompson said she watched as the local health department failed to distinguish which types of masks help with smoke issues (N95 masks are better at filtering out tiny particles; cloth or surgical masks are less effective). So with her fellow organizers at Mendo Clean Air Club, she began partnering with local businesses that offered to distribute masks, too. Mendo Clean Air Club is one of over 40 clean air clubs around the world. Launched by Emily Dupree, a Chicago resident, the first club lent out air purifiers to touring musicians during Covid. Now, Clean Air Clubs and Mask Blocs – a mutual aid practice for sharing masks – are offering free masks and air purifiers from their “lending libraries” to help their local communities stay safe from wildfire smoke and monitor air quality. Mask Bloc Los Angeles, for example, handed out more than 300,000 masks in two weeks during the catastrophic January 2025 LA fires. “Covid and climate change are two major pillars of collective denial in the last decade,” said Dupree. “So though our lending library was created in response to one kind of public failure – namely a failure of public health, which is still ongoing – it can serve as a solution in response to this second failure, of governments to adequately address the growing threat of climate change, of worsening wildfires and worsening air quality.” When wildfire smoke was negatively affecting Chicago air quality in July, Dupree noticed that their lending library of 15 purifiers was not fully booked. “It just didn’t sit right with me,” she said. So they started encouraging people struggling with the smoke to reserve purifiers, which they could retrieve from a storage unit; within hours, the library was fully booked, she said. “We are able to mobilize clean air resources extremely quickly because we are not dealing with bureaucracy or red tape,” Dupree said. “We just get the purifiers placed where they’re needed as quickly as possible.” This speed and access are particularly helpful for populations with underlying health conditions. When then-president Joe Biden declared the Covid emergency “over” in 2023, Shannon Durkin, a Mask Bloc Delaware organizer – who is especially vulnerable due to her cystic fibrosis – thought her life was functionally over, too. Since the first US lockdown in March 2020, and the ensuing anti-public health backlash, she’s felt excised from participating in public life. She has faced discrimination when going out in her respirator, surrounded by collective denial that Covid and other viral illnesses are still dangerous. In 2024, Durkin and her husband Jimmy helped launch Mask Bloc Delaware, distributing KN95 masks at protests and partnering with other organizing groups, such as the local Food Not Bombs and DSA chapters. In July, they walked around Wilmington, Delaware, as wildfire smoke from Canada permeated the east coast to distribute PPE. The Durkins said people were surprisingly enthusiastic about receiving it, not even realizing the possible health risks of the air quality. They were also able to drop masks off at various local businesses for distribution. Organizers say the work of Clean Air Clubs and Mask Blocs feels more necessary than ever, as the current administration continues to cast doubt on the usefulness of masks and the severity of the Covid pandemic that in 2020 killed more than 350,000 Americans. Thompson said she navigates any Covid hesitancy by explaining to residents how it can affect their health, their families and their livelihoods. “The big message that’s gotten through in a rural, underfunded region is that we can’t afford to get sick or to get long Covid,” said Thompson. “A lot of us are manual laborers or use our bodies for work in some way. We just don’t have the resources here to manage that.” Awareness of Clean Air Clubs continues to grow; Dupree even created a Google doc breaking down how others can start their own. Organizers say being part of these mutual aid groups can offer hope in a time of hopelessness. “A lot of people, when they’re looking at the various horrors of the world, can feel overwhelmed and then stuck regarding what they should do about it,” said Dupree. “But what this shows us is that even if you decide to focus on one problem, it turns out usually what you come up with is going to be able to pivot and solve other problems that you didn’t initially try to address. There’s a kind of freedom in that.”

title: Italy condemns Spain’s ‘unacceptable’ border controls as Ceuta fallout intensifies
summary: Travellers caught up in migration row as Madrid introduces checks on visitors from Italy in retaliation for Rome’s move
body: Italy’s foreign minister has called Spain’s decision to impose retaliatory checks on travellers from Italy “incomprehensible and completely unacceptable” as people making their way between the two EU countries were left grappling with the effects of the escalating feud. Spain started carrying out spot checks on visitors from Italy at midnight on Saturday. The tit-for-tat move came after Rome infuriated Madrid by launching checks on 1 August for travellers from Spain in response to the recent influx of about 72,000 people into Ceuta, a Spanish territory in north Africa. Spanish officials were swift to point out that the Italian checks made little sense, given that by 1 August, the border in Ceuta was back under control and the vast majority of those who had arrived had been returned to Morocco. Ceuta is not part of the Schengen free-movement zone, Madrid has repeatedly stressed, meaning there is little chance of onward travel to continental Europe without EU citizenship or residency. The checks by Italy had led to “intolerable” scenes at Italian airports, Spain’s foreign minister, José Manuel Albares, told reporters. “This measure is, first and foremost, an attack on the dignity of the Spanish people, but, secondly, it is a torpedo fired at the hull of European unity,” he said. In an interview published on Sunday in La Stampa, Italy’s foreign minister defended the move by Rome. “Some order needs to be brought in: we’re not against Spain, but we have a duty to protect our borders,” said Antonio Tajani, voicing concerns about some of the migrants potentially holding jihadist views. “What is incomprehensible and completely unacceptable is Spain’s reaction.” He pushed back against the suggestion that Rome’s actions were symbolic, given the remote possibility of anyone making it to Italy from Ceuta. “Where do they go after arriving in Spain? Italy, as a destination, is the country most at risk. We’re not Germany or Norway.” When asked if Italy’s response was proportionate, Tajani pointed to the reports of fresh calls online for a mid-August mass crossing. “We hope to be able to lift the suspension soon, as soon as the risk is no longer present,” he said. Italy’s interior minister publicly praised Spain last week for its handling of the crisis, but Tajani blasted Spain for not being “as vigilant” as it should have been. He linked the influx to Spain’s recent regularisation programme, describing the move to provide working migrants with papers as a “negative message that puts everyone’s safety at risk,” despite the EU’s earlier dismissal of any connection between the Ceuta influx and regularisation. Italy’s government has long criticised Spain’s efforts to regularise undocumented migrants, even as it quietly works on similar plans to give nearly 1.1 million work permits to foreign workers by 2028. Speaking to the Financial Times, one researcher described the Italian government’s efforts as a “disguised amnesty.” Spain and Italy both have a long history of regularisation programmes. In 2002, Tajani’s party, Forza Italia, carried out one of Italy’s largest such programmes, issuing just over 634,000 permits. Even so, the perception of differences in their approach to migration has pitted Madrid and Rome against each other, with Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, seeking to position herself as a hardliner on migration while Spain’s Pedro Sánchez – who has defended the need for foreign workers to grow Spain’s economy and stave off demographic collapse – said Italy had registered the highest number of irregular crossings in recent years in the EU, with figures that are double those of Spain. In recent days, the row has widened to include people making their way between the two countries, a route used by more than 8 million last year. “It’s ridiculous that we’re in this situation,” Elisa Fabbri, 41, told Spanish news site Eldiario.es as she left Madrid-Barajas airport on Saturday. Israel Pérez, a Cuban-born Spanish citizen, described it as an “absurd spiral” that risked pulling everyone down. “If we keep imposing checks on each other, in the end we’ll all end up losing,” he said. “This shouldn’t be happening between two European countries.” In Italy, opposition politicians accused Meloni of unleashing an “unfounded diplomatic crisis” that would ultimately harm Italians. “The cynical propaganda of the Meloni government has produced what was predictable: a boomerang that Italians will pay dearly for,” said Nicola Fratoianni, the leader of the Greens and Left Alliance. “This is a colossal mistake.” The EU commissioner for migration, Magnus Brunner, said on Saturday that he had been in contact with the interior ministers of the two countries. “Both confirmed that the internal border controls are temporary,” he said on social media. “Spanish authorities assured us the events in Ceuta will have no lasting effect on the Schengen area. That is why there are signals from Italy that controls could be lifted soon.” The row between Rome and Madrid after the events in Ceuta hints at sensitivities over migration across the EU, particularly as governments in Italy, France and Poland prepare to face off against far-right challengers in upcoming elections. But the latest Eurobarometer poll, which tracks public opinions every quarter, suggests the focus on migration may be out of step with Europeans’ top priorities. When asked about the topics that should be a priority for the European parliament, migration ranked sixth, behind issues such as the cost of living, the defence and security of the EU and the economy and job creation.
